Technical design, innovation and their consequences play a pivotal role in the current transformation towards sustainable development of society. The course aims to equip students with skills and offer perspectives that extend beyond specialized expertise as this alone is not sufficient to effectively contribute to socially responsible societies and processes. The course content and learning outcomes encourage critical thinking on dominant systems and assumptions through reflecting on for instance existing power constellations, vested interests, and norm conflicts.

To navigate complex challenges, future professionals should master key sustainability competencies that allow them to effectively approach complexity in transdisciplinary circumstances. This requires understanding of how values influence processes and decisions (values-thinking), how problems are interconnected and cannot be viewed in isolation (systems-thinking), how envisioning different potential futures can help promote long-term sustainability (futures-thinking) to foster strategic and transformative change.

Continuous reflection on group work, continuous analysis of case development, case dissemination as relevant (paper/poster/seminar/presentation/peer-feedback).

Course syllabus
Critical Thinking and Complex Systems: Challenges and Futures
Kritiskt tänkande och komplexa system: utmaningar och framtid
MXLN01, 7.5 credits, A (Second Cycle)

Valid for: 2026/27
Faculty: Faculty of Engineering LTH
Decided by: PLED M
Date of Decision: 2026-03-26
    
  
General Information

Main field:  Technology
      
      
        Depth of study relative to the degree requirements:  Second cycle, in-depth level of the course cannot be classified
      
      
Elective for: B4, BME4, BR4, C4, D4, E4, F4, I4, K4, N4, Pi4, R4, W4
Language of instruction: The course will be given in English on demand
    
  
Aim
Technical design, innovation and their consequences play a pivotal role in the current transformation towards sustainable development of society. The course aims to equip students with skills and offer perspectives that extend beyond specialized expertise as this alone is not sufficient to effectively contribute to socially responsible societies and processes. The course content and learning outcomes encourage critical thinking on dominant systems and assumptions through reflecting on for instance existing power constellations, vested interests, and norm conflicts. To navigate complex challenges, future professionals should master key sustainability competencies that allow them to effectively approach complexity in transdisciplinary circumstances. This requires understanding of how values influence processes and decisions (values-thinking), how problems are interconnected and cannot be viewed in isolation (systems-thinking), how envisioning different potential futures can help promote long-term sustainability (futures-thinking) to foster strategic and transformative change.
Learning outcomes
Knowledge and understanding
      For a passing grade the student must
Discuss sustainability aspects of societal and/or socio-technical issues and their interconnectedness in a coherent, well-developed and non-superficial way. Describe the impact of different relevant worldviews and discuss some inherent and relevant polarities with respect to societal issues. 
Competences and skills
      For a passing grade the student must
Apply systems thinking in order to identify and understand key elements such as relevant trade-offs, present and historical priorities and power structures.    Construct and engage with future visions including critical uncertainties and consider alternative development pathways. Integrate knowledge and insights critically and systematically to develop elements of a transition strategy. 
Judgement and approach
      For a passing grade the student must
Advance effective collaboration competency through iterative reflection.  Engage in critical thinking across perspectives based on recognizing and respecting yours and others’ values, needs and circumstances. Reflect on and argue for a personal view on professional responsibility and change agency.  
Contents
Futures thinking: examples of futuring techniques such as backcastingSystems thinking: linkage of historical development to present systems, mapping causes and consequences, leverage and intervention points.Values thinking: principles, norms and trade-offs including concepts such as justice and responsibility in various processes.Strategies thinking: Planning under uncertainty, complexity with respect to sociotechnical issues. Team and individual growth: awareness of own competence and contribution, through goal setting activities, evaluation, peer feedback and reflexive practices.Communication and argumentation: Effective, authentic and clear argumentation aiming at meaningful sense-making with respect to complex issues.
Examination details

Grading scale: UG - (U, G) - (Fail, Pass)
Assessment: Preparation according to instructions for discussion seminars and workshops. Submission of quizzes, written reflections and analyses in due time. Active participation in seminars and workshops. Continuous reflection on group work, continuous analysis of case development, case dissemination as relevant (paper/poster/seminar/presentation/peer-feedback).Peer feedback, showing independent application of course methods and theories in writing and/or orally. 

The examiner, in consultation with Disability Support Services, may deviate from the regular form of examination in order to provide a permanently disabled student with a form of examination equivalent to that of a student without a disability.

Modules
Code: 0126. Name: Reflections, Hand-ins, Quizzes and Seminars/Workshops.. 

Credits: 4.0. Grading scale: UG - (U, G).
        
          Assessment: Relevant preparation for discussion seminars and workshops. Submission of quizzes, written reflections and if relevant other texts in due time. Active participation in seminars and workshops. 
        
        
          The module includes: Seminars concerning the course content and workshops with relevance for the course learning outcomes. Reflections and quizzes related to progression within the course.
        
        
        
Code: 0226. Name: Case. 

Credits: 3.5. Grading scale: UG - (U, G).
        
          Assessment: Continuous reflection on group work, continuous case analysis development, case dissemination as relevant (paper/poster/seminar/presentation/peer-feedback).
        
        
          The module includes: Case work. The case analysis is successively developed using the skills developed during the course. Continuous assessment of group work. 
        
        
        

Admission

Admission requirements: 

120 credits within the programme syllabus

Assumed prior knowledge: 
        Experience with group project work
        
The number of participants is limited to: 50
Selection: Completed university credits within the programme. Priority is given to students enrolled on programmes that include the course in their curriculum. 
The course might be cancelled:  if the number of applicants is less than 10.

Reading list

The course literature consists of electronic materials freely available within LU, such as articles, excerpts from e-books, etc. The reading list will be made available well in time with respect to the course start.

Contact

Course coordinator: Carina Fasth,
        carina.fasth@ftf.lth.se

Further information
Course literature will typically be in English and teachers that do not speak Swedish may be part of the teaching team. Individual student hand-ins can likely be in Swedish regardless of course language.
